summary:
SELENE-LOLA is an intuitive mission planning and ephemeris web application designed to evaluate candidate landing sites and launch windows for NASA’s Artemis and Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) missions to the Moon's South Pole.

Because the Moon’s 1.54° axial tilt creates extreme low-grazing solar angles and severe terrain shadows, mission feasibility shifts drastically with minor coordinate or schedule adjustments. SELENE-LOLA bridges the gap between raw datasets and agile mission design by translating NASA JPL Horizons ephemerides and Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) topographic models into clear, interactive visual interfaces.

Our solution provides:

An interactive Stereographic Sky Radar and 360° Panoramic Skyline showing real-time Sun and Earth horizon clearance.
An interactive 3D spaceflight surface simulator with tracking solar arrays, steerable comms dishes, and multiple camera views.
A real-time hardware feasibility engine calculating solar array electrical output (Watts), RF link budget margins (dB), and Stefan-Boltzmann thermal regimes.
A side-by-side site trade-off matrix with synchronized 30-day temporal scrubbers.

SELENE-LOLA empowers mission planners, educators, and the public to rapidly assess power availability and direct-to-Earth communication windows to ensure lunar mission success
details:
1. What Does It Do & How Does It Work?

SELENE-LOLA is an interactive, high-precision lunar mission planning and visualization platform designed to evaluate candidate landing sites at the Moon’s south pole. The tool models the complex lighting and communication environment by calculating real-time topocentric Sun and Earth positions relative to the local horizon.

The platform works through four integrated calculation and visualization layers:

  • Astrodynamics & Ephemeris Engine: Implements NASA JPL Horizons-grade analytical planetary theory (Jean Meeus algorithm) combined with Cassini’s 1.5424° polar rotation model and optical/physical lunar libration (wobbling ±6.7° in latitude and ±8.1° in longitude). It transforms selenocentric vectors into topocentric spherical coordinates (Azimuth 0°–360°, Elevation relative to the local horizon) without atmospheric refraction.
  • Topographic Horizon Masking: Integrates Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) elevation profiles to calculate true local skyline obstructions caused by steep crater rims and peaks of eternal light.
  • Mission Feasibility Engine: Evaluates real-time power generation across three solar panel geometries (vertical tracking masts, fixed vertical arrays, and flat horizontal decks), computes Direct-to-Earth (DTE) RF link budgets and carrier margins (+dB), and models Stefan-Boltzmann equilibrium thermal regimes (40 K to 387 K).
  • Multi-Modal Visualizations: Presents data through a stereographic sky radar, a 360° panoramic horizon skyline, dual cartographic projections (South Polar Stereographic -90° to -65° and Global Selenographic), and a real-time 3D surface spaceflight simulator.

2. What Benefits Does It Have?

  • Instant Agile Re-Planning: When launch delays or hardware setbacks occur, mission planners can shift landing dates and locations across 30-day lunar illumination cycles in seconds, instantly viewing the impact on sunlight duration and communication availability.
  • Side-by-Side Trade-Off Analysis: Features a dual-site comparison matrix (e.g., Shackleton Connecting Ridge vs. Malapert Mountain vs. Nobile VIPER Rim) that synchronizes timelines to identify optimal operational windows.
  • Elimination of Workflow Bottlenecks: Replaces the need to cross-reference multiple disjointed, technical interfaces (such as NASA QuickMap, Moon Trek, and command-line JPL Horizons queries) with an all-in-one, unified mission control interface.
  • Preventing Critical Engineering Oversights: Graphically demonstrates key polar realities—such as showing that horizontal solar arrays experience a ~97% power loss compared to vertical tracking masts, and that lunar libration can drop Earth below crater rims even when the lunar landing site is nominally facing Earth.

3. What Is the Intended Impact?

  • Supporting NASA Artemis & CLPS: Streamlines site selection trade-offs for commercial lunar landers (Intuitive Machines, Astrobotic), rovers (VIPER), and crewed Artemis missions.
  • Bridging Science & Engineering: Coordinates the competing priorities of science teams (seeking water ice deposits deep within cryogenic, permanently shadowed craters) and engineering teams (requiring line-of-sight communication and continuous solar power along crater rims).
  • STEM Engagement & Education: Makes intricate celestial mechanics and lunar surface challenges accessible and compelling to students, educators, and the public worldwide.

4. Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software Used

  • Languages & Core Framework: TypeScript, React 18, HTML5, Modern CSS (Tailwind CSS).
  • 3D Simulation & Graphics: Three.js, WebGL, custom GLSL lighting shaders, procedural starfield with 4,500+ stars, and photorealistic Earth Rayleigh limb atmospheric shaders.
  • Development & Build Environment: Vite 5, Node.js, PowerShell, Git.
  • Mathematical & Data Models: Analytical Meeus Planetary Ephemeris, NASA Cassini Rotation Model, LOLA (Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter) Topographic Grids, Stefan-Boltzmann Radiation Laws, Friis Free-Space RF Path Loss Equations.
  • Icons & UI Telemetry: Lucide React, SVG vector radar rendering, and Canvas 2D cartographic projections.
  • Presentation Tooling: Python 3 and python-pptx for generating the compliant 7-slide demo deck.

5. How Is Your Project Creative?

  • Kerbal Space Program-Inspired Spaceflight Experience: Integrates a responsive 3D spaceflight simulator featuring an authentic Artemis/CLPS lunar lander (gold MLI thermal insulation, RCS thruster pods, steerable Earth-tracking parabolic comms dish with active RF carrier visualization, and vertical solar array wings) and a deployed ALSEP surface science station.
  • Flight-Grade KSP NavBall: Implements a realistic spherical NavBall (SURF mode) displaying pitch, roll, and artificial horizon orientation, coupled with multiple flight camera perspectives (Orbital Free-Cam, Astronaut Cockpit POV, Ground Station, and Top-Down Recon).
  • Aerospace Mission Control Aesthetic: Designed with deep blue, slate, and high-contrast cyan/gold telemetry panels that evoke modern space operations centers.

6. What Factors Did Your Team Consider?

  • Absence of Lunar Atmosphere: Horizons are governed strictly by planetary curvature and local topographic elevation rather than atmospheric refraction.
  • Extreme Polar Thermal Regimes: Surface temperatures swing from 40 Kelvin (-233°C) in shadowed crater bottoms to 387 Kelvin (+114°C) under direct sun, requiring survival heater calculations during twilight transitions.
  • Lunar Libration Dynamics: The Moon’s tidal wobble causes Earth to oscillate in the polar sky by up to 13.4° over a synodic month, meaning Earth line-of-sight is dynamic rather than static.
  • Multi-Tier User Accessibility: Designed with a dual-layer UX: high-level Flight Readiness Badges (GO / CAUTION / NO-GO) for non-specialists and educators, paired with raw numeric telemetry (elevation angles, dB link margins, Watt yields, and Kelvin temperatures) for aerospace engineers.
